2027-05-14.title: Seventh Friday of Resurrection · St Matthias, Apostle (Mar Mathias Shleeha)
2027-05-14.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The LORD looks on the heart: David is anointed
Matthias is added to the eleven apostles
God chose what is weak in the world
Revealed to infants; come to me and find rest
2027-05-14.alt: Season of the Resurrection (Qyamta). The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and the Queen of Heaven (Regina Caeli) is prayed in place of the Angelus until Pentecost. These are the days between the Ascension and Pentecost, when the Church, like the apostles with Mary in the upper room, prays for the coming of the Holy Spirit. St Matthias the Apostle (the calendar spells the name Mathias) is listed in the First Set with the readings above; the calendar gives the longer form 1 Samuel 16:1–13. Weekday readings of the Seventh Friday: 1 John 2:22–25; Matthew 24:7–14. In the Latin calendar St Matthias is also kept today, as a feast. Follow the direction of the eparchy and parish on which readings are used (verify locally).
2027-05-14.verse: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias; and he was added to the eleven apostles.
theo: Today the Church remembers an apostle about whom Scripture tells us one story only, and that story happens in these very days. Between the Ascension and Pentecost the eleven return to Jerusalem and go up to the upper room, and Luke tells us that “All these were constantly devoting themselves to prayer, together with certain women, including Mary the mother of Jesus, as well as his brothers” (Acts 1:14). The next verse begins: “In those days Peter stood up among the believers (together the crowd numbered about one hundred twenty persons)”. So the choice of Matthias is made by a praying Church, gathered around the Mother of the Lord, waiting for the Spirit. Peter, who had denied his Master three times and been forgiven by the lakeshore, now acts as the shepherd Jesus made him. He does not hide the painful wound: Judas “was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” The place left empty by betrayal must be filled, because the Twelve are not a random committee. Jesus had chosen twelve, as Israel had twelve tribes, and had promised: “you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28). The new Israel needs its twelve foundations before the Spirit comes.

Peter states what an apostle must be: “one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us”. And then the heart of the matter: “one of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection.” An apostle is first of all a witness, someone who has walked with Jesus and seen him risen. Two names are proposed: Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. Then the community prays: “Lord, you know everyone’s heart. Show us which one of these two you have chosen”. Notice the words: not whom we prefer, but whom you have chosen. They cast lots, an old way in Israel of leaving the decision to God (“The lot is cast into the lap, but the decision is the LORD’s alone,” Proverbs 16:33), and the lot falls on Matthias. It is the last time Scripture shows the Church choosing by lot; after Pentecost the Spirit will guide her through prayer, discernment and the laying on of hands. Joseph Justus, not chosen, disappears from the story without a word of complaint, a quiet lesson for every one of us who is passed over. Ancient tradition is uncertain about where Matthias later preached and died; Eusebius records the opinion that he had been one of the seventy disciples, and a tradition holds that his relics rest in Trier in Germany, where an abbey bears his name. We know little about him; we know the one thing that matters: he was chosen by the Lord to witness to the Resurrection.

The first reading for the feast explains how God chooses. Samuel comes to Bethlehem to anoint a king among the sons of Jesse. He sees Eliab, tall and impressive, and thinks, surely this is the one. “But the LORD said to Samuel, ‘Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for the LORD does not see as mortals see; they look on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.’” Seven sons pass by, and none is chosen. “Are all your sons here?” “There remains yet the youngest, but he is keeping the sheep.” The boy nobody thought to call is the one God has chosen; Samuel anoints him, “and the spirit of the LORD came mightily upon David from that day forward.” The pattern is clear: God looks on the heart, chooses the one who seems least, and then gives his Spirit. Paul writes the same truth to the proud Corinthians: “Consider your own call, brothers and sisters: not many of you were wise by human standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong”. Why? “so that no one might boast in the presence of God.” Our worth is not in our talents but in Christ, “who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption”.

The Gospel lets us hear Jesus praying with joy: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants”. The fishermen of Galilee, the tax collector, the zealot, and now Matthias, were such infants: not learned men, but men to whom the Father had revealed the Son. Then comes the invitation that every apostle has carried to the ends of the earth: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart”. The apostolic office is not a crown but a yoke shared with Christ; bishops, priests and every baptised person who serves learn from the gentle and humble heart of Jesus or they do not learn at all. Our Syro-Malabar Church calls herself the Church of the Mar Thoma Christians, proud of her apostolic origin. Today's feast reminds us that apostolic faith rests not on our pride but on God's choice and on the witness to the Resurrection handed down from those first Twelve. The weekday readings echo the same call: “Let what you heard from the beginning abide in you” (1 John 2:24), and “the one who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24:13). Matthias stayed with Jesus from the beginning, and endured to the end.
conn: Jesus promised the Twelve that “you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:28); the number must be complete before Pentecost.
Peter applies the psalm to Judas: “‘Let another take his position of overseer.’” (Acts 1:20).
“You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last” (John 15:16).
“He chose his servant David, and took him from the sheepfolds” (Psalm 78:70); the youngest son, keeping the sheep, is anointed.

Peter later tells Cornelius that the Risen Lord appeared “not to all the people but to us who were chosen by God as witnesses, and who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10:41).
On David “the spirit of the LORD came mightily” after his anointing (1 Samuel 16:13); on Matthias and the eleven the Spirit will come at Pentecost (Acts 2:4).
altar: At every Holy Qurbana we pray in communion with the apostles, whose faith our Church received through Mar Thoma. The bishop who presides in our eparchy stands in the line of those Twelve, completed on this day by Matthias.
The Lord who chose the least of Jesse's sons and the unknown Matthias chooses us also to come to his altar; at Communion he says again, Come to me, and I will give you rest.
outline: An apostle known for one story only, chosen in the days of waiting with Mary.
Point 1 · The place must be filled
The Twelve and the twelve tribes; the wound of Judas healed by the praying Church.
Point 2 · A witness to his resurrection
Walking with Jesus from the beginning, and the lot that falls on Matthias.
Point 3 · The LORD looks on the heart
David the youngest, and the weak chosen to shame the strong.
The gentle yoke that every apostle carries.
Joseph Justus, not chosen, going home in peace and still praying with the Church.
live: Before any decision today, at work or at home, pray: Lord, you know the heart; show me what you have chosen.
Do not look on appearance (1 Samuel 16:7)
Notice today someone usually overlooked, and give that person your time and respect.
If you are not chosen, not thanked or not noticed today, offer it quietly like Joseph Justus.
Bring one heavy burden to the Lord in prayer this evening and leave it with him.
fathers: Peter, as the first of the apostles, could have chosen alone, yet he acts with all the brethren, so that the choice may be beyond dispute. They pray, “You know the hearts”, for they wanted not their own choice but the Lord's; and they rightly place the decision in the hands of God, since the Spirit had not yet come.

The apostles received the Gospel from the Lord Jesus Christ, and Christ was sent from God. Having been filled with the Holy Spirit, they preached and appointed those who would succeed them, so that the ministry would continue in the Church in good order.
magis: The Lord Jesus endowed his community with a structure: the choice of the Twelve with Peter as their head. Representing the twelve tribes of Israel, they are the foundation stones of the new Jerusalem.
The Church is apostolic because she is founded on the apostles, chosen witnesses sent out on mission by Christ himself.
In order that the mission entrusted to them might be continued after their death, the apostles consigned to their immediate collaborators the duty of completing the work they had begun.
Throughout the Old Covenant God prepared the mission of Mary; against all human expectation he chooses those considered powerless and weak to show his faithfulness.
The Word became flesh to be our model of holiness: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me.”
saints: St Matthias, Apostle (Mar Mathias Shleeha), chosen by lot to take the place of Judas among the Twelve (Acts 1:15–26). In the Latin calendar a feast on the same day (since 1969; formerly 24 February).

14–16 May: the last days of the Season of the Resurrection. Fri 14: St Matthias, Apostle (Mar Mathias Shleeha), kept the same day in the Latin calendar. Sat 15: Blessed Virgin Mary, Protectress of Harvest, an important Marian feast; in the Latin Church the Vigil of Pentecost is celebrated in the evening. Sun 16: First Sunday of the Apostles, the Feast of Pentecost; the Season of the Apostles begins.
2027-05-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you chose the Twelve to be witnesses of your Resurrection, and when one place was left empty you filled it through the prayer of your Church gathered with your Mother. Through the prayers of Mar Mathias Shleeha and of Mar Thoma our father in faith, keep our Church faithful to the apostolic faith. You look on the heart and not on appearance: purify our hearts, teach us to accept your choices without envy, and give us your gentle and humble heart. As we wait with Mary for the Holy Spirit, make us witnesses of your Resurrection in our homes and our work. Glory to you, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen. Alleluia!

catechism: The Twelve, foundation of the new Israel.
The Church built on the apostles.
kidsaint: After Judas left, there were only eleven apostles, and Jesus had chosen twelve. So the friends of Jesus prayed together with Mother Mary, and asked God to show them who should be the twelfth. They chose Matthias, a man who had followed Jesus from the very beginning and had seen him risen. Lesson: God sees our heart, and he can choose anyone who loves Jesus faithfully!
2027-05-14.special: St Matthias, Apostle (Mar Mathias Shleeha). Seventh Friday of Resurrection.
term: From the Greek apostolos and the Syriac shlīḥā, both meaning one who is sent. The Twelve were chosen by Jesus to be with him and to be sent out as witnesses of his Resurrection; our Church calls them Shleehe, and the Season of the Apostles that begins at Pentecost bears their name. The bishops are their successors.

family.explain: After Jesus went up to heaven, his friends waited in Jerusalem and prayed with Mother Mary. One place among the twelve apostles was empty, because Judas had left. Peter said they needed someone who had walked with Jesus from the beginning and had seen him alive after Easter. They prayed: “Lord, you know everyone’s heart.” Then God showed them Matthias. God sees what is inside us, not only what is outside.
family.intention: We pray for our bishops and priests, that they may be faithful witnesses of Jesus like the apostles.
family.ask: Ask: “When we have to decide something as a family, do we first pray and ask God what he wants?”

illus: In 2012 the Coptic Orthodox Church of Egypt chose a new Pope in the ancient way. After much prayer, the names of three candidates were placed in a sealed box on the altar, and during the liturgy a small boy, blindfolded, drew out one name. The man chosen, Bishop Tawadros, accepted it as the Lord's choice. Many watching in Egypt wept as the name was read. It was the scene of Acts 1 repeated: a Church at prayer, a decision placed in the Lord's hands, and a chosen servant who did not choose himself.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you chose your apostles and you know every heart. As we gather in your name with your Mother, make us one in prayer like the Church in the upper room. Amen. Alleluia!
share: Lord, you know everyone’s heart (Acts 1:24). What does the Lord see in my heart today?
One of these must become a witness with us to his resurrection (Acts 1:22). Where am I called to witness to the Risen Lord?
The LORD does not see as mortals see (1 Samuel 16:7). Whom have I judged by appearance?
Come to me, all you that are weary (Matthew 11:28). What burden do I want to give to Jesus tonight?
pm.resp: Lord, you know our hearts; show us your will.
interc: For our Major Archbishop, our bishops and all successors of the apostles, that they may be faithful witnesses of the Risen Lord.
For those preparing for priesthood and religious life, that they may hear the Lord's choice and answer with joy.
For those who have been passed over or forgotten, that they may know God's love for them.
For all who are weary and burdened, that they may find rest in Christ.
For our families and parishes, that we may pray together as we wait for the Holy Spirit.
pm.close: Father, you completed the number of the apostles by choosing Matthias in the place of Judas. Number us also among the faithful witnesses of your Son, and fill us with the Holy Spirit whom we await. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. Alleluia!

homily: Dear friends, today we keep the feast of St Matthias, Mar Mathias Shleeha. We know only one story about him, and it happened in these very days, between the Ascension and Pentecost, when the apostles were praying in the upper room with Mary the mother of Jesus (Acts 1:14).

Judas had betrayed the Lord, and one of the twelve places was empty. Peter stood up and said that someone who had walked with Jesus from the beginning must become “a witness with us to his resurrection” (Acts 1:22). That is what an apostle is: a witness of the Risen Lord.

They proposed two men, Joseph Justus and Matthias, and they prayed: “Lord, you know everyone’s heart. Show us which one of these two you have chosen” (Acts 1:24). Not whom we like, but whom you have chosen. The lot fell on Matthias. And Joseph Justus went home without complaint. Both are lessons for us.

Samuel thought the tall Eliab must be God's choice, but God said: “the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). The youngest boy, out with the sheep, was anointed. Paul says the same: God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, so that no one may boast before God (1 Corinthians 1:27–29).

Jesus thanks the Father for revealing these things to infants, and he invites: “Come to me, all you that are weary… and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The apostles were simple men who learned from his gentle and humble heart. Our Church, the Church of Mar Thoma, received the faith from such apostles.

Let us pray before our decisions, as the first Church did. Let us not judge by appearance. And as we wait with Mary for the Holy Spirit, let us be witnesses of the Resurrection, each in our own place. Alleluia! Amen.
kids: Children, there were twelve apostles, but one left Jesus. So the others prayed with Mother Mary and asked God to choose a new apostle. God chose Matthias!
God does not look at how tall or strong or clever we are. He looks at our heart. Let us keep our heart full of love for Jesus.
